title: Ewa Agoyin
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: Beans boiled without salt so they cook faster, then salted and boiled on until they collapse — mashed until almost no whole bean is left in sight.
longDesc: The beans half of ewa agoyin is almost absurdly simple and the technique is in the order of operations. Salt goes in only once the beans are tender, because salting early slows them down; then they keep boiling until they are very soft, and a wooden spoon takes them the rest of the way. The target is explicit — mash until there is almost no whole bean in sight. What you want is a loose, grey-brown, structureless mass, which is exactly the right backdrop for the very dark pepper sauce that goes on top.
ingredients: Salt, added only once the beans are tender
steps: Pick over the beans and wash them.
Cover generously with water and cook until tender, without adding any salt — the beans cook faster this way.
When they are tender, add salt.
Use a wooden spoon to mash the beans until there is almost no whole bean in sight.
Serve hot under the agoyin sauce (NGA031), with agege bread (NGA036).
chefTips: No salt until tender. The reason given is simply that the beans cook faster — and it is the opposite of what another named source does, boiling everything together from the start.
Go past tender. Ewa agoyin beans are not meant to hold their shape at all.
Mash in the pot with a wooden spoon, over low heat. Off the heat it stiffens and resists.
Keep it loose. It will tighten as it sits, and the sauce needs something to sink into.
Black-eyed beans here, though Nigerian honey beans — ewa oloyin — are the sweeter traditional choice and are widely preferred.
Make much more sauce than you think you need. The beans are plain by design and the whole dish is the ratio of sauce to beans.
Agege bread is not optional in Lagos. The beans go into a split loaf and that is the street version.
commonMistakes: Stopping at tender rather than collapsed.
sources: Adapted from the beans half of 'Ewa Agoyin And Agoyin Sauce Recipe (VIDEO)', byline Sisi Jemimah. Quantity as printed: 3 cups Black Eyed Beans. The method is as printed: 'cook until tender without adding salt initially "so the beans cooks faster"'; when tender add salt; 'continue boiling until very soft, then use a wooden spoon to mash the beans till there's almost no whole beans in sight.' Yield not specified.

Her headnote: 'Growing up, the combination of Ewa Agoyin and the Ewa Agoyin sauce served with it had to be the best thing that ever happened to my beans diet.' She describes weekend hawkers and wanting to recreate the authentic recipe at home.

DISAGREEMENT on the beans, not reconciled. She withholds salt to speed the cooking; 1Q Food Platter boils everything together — beans, onion, seasoning and salt — for 30 minutes flat (NGA032). Her stated rationale is directly contradicted by the other's practice. Lola Osinkolu cooks 1 lb of beans in 6 to 8 cups of water for 2 to 2 1/2 hours until very tender and mashes to preference (NGA033).

ON THE DISH'S ORIGIN: ewa agoyin is Yoruba-adopted rather than Yoruba-origin. BusinessDay attributes it to the Agoyin or Aganyin people of Benin and Togo, carried into Lagos — which is why it is filed here under Agoyin (Lagos) rather than Yoruba. That also fits the finding that most of the Lagos Island snack trade is run by women from Benin Republic and Togo.
The sauce is the other half of this dish and is published separately at NGA031 because the bleach-or-don't-bleach disagreement belongs to the sauce, not the beans.
reheating: Low heat with water to loosen. It sets solid when cold.
healthBenefits: Cowpeas supply plant protein, folate, iron and soluble fibre.
No fat at all in the beans themselves.
culturalNote: Ewa agoyin is Lagos street breakfast and the name carries its history: the Agoyin people of Benin and Togo brought it, and Lagosians adopted it so completely that it now reads as a Lagos dish. It is sold from a wheelbarrow or a basin with a loaf of agege bread beside it, and the sauce — black, oily and fierce — is what people queue for.
